concept_card.statement: Light bends toward the normal entering a denser medium, away entering a rarer one; TIR needs denser-to-rarer travel beyond the critical angle.
concept_card.analogy: A cycle rolling slantwise onto sand turns one way; back onto road, the other way.
steps: Denser side: ray nearer the normal
Denser to rarer? sin C = n2/n1
TIR only if incidence angle exceeds C
concept_card.worked_example: Glass to air, n = 1.5: sin C = 1/1.5, C ≈ 41.8°. At 45° inside: TIR. At 30°: exits at 48.6°.
concept_card.subtopic: Refraction at a plane surface and total internal reflection
concept_card.learning_objective: Predict whether a ray bends toward or away from the normal, use n = c/v and Snell's law, and decide when total internal reflection can occur.
concept_card.simple: Light slows down in glass or water and speeds up again in air. Slowing down makes it bend toward the normal; speeding up makes it bend away. If light inside glass or water meets the surface at too steep an angle, it cannot get out and reflects back completely: total internal reflection.
concept_card.formal: The refractive index of a medium is n = c/v, the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium. At a boundary, Snell's law n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r fixes the refracted direction. Frequency is set by the source and stays the same, so the wavelength becomes λ_vacuum/n. For travel from a denser to a rarer medium, the critical angle C obeys sin C = n₂/n₁; for incidence beyond C there is no refracted ray and all the light is reflected.

equations.meaning: Refractive index compares the speed of light in vacuum with its speed in the medium.

vars.v: speed of light in the medium (m/s)

equations.expr: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r
equations.meaning: Snell's law links the angles on the two sides of a boundary.

vars.n₁: refractive index of first medium (no unit)
vars.n₂: refractive index of second medium (no unit)
vars.i: angle of incidence from the normal (degree)
vars.r: angle of refraction from the normal (degree)

equations.assumptions: Angles measured from the normal; plane boundary.

equations.meaning: Wavelength shrinks by the factor n while frequency stays fixed.
equations.assumptions: Frequency is set by the source and does not change at a boundary.

equations.expr: sin C = n₂ / n₁ (= 1/n into air)
equations.meaning: Critical angle beyond which total internal reflection occurs.

vars.n₁: refractive index of denser medium (no unit)
vars.n₂: refractive index of rarer medium (no unit)

equations.assumptions: Only defined for n₁ > n₂, light travelling denser to rarer; TIR when i > C.

alternatives: Wavefront view: one edge of a slanting wavefront reaches the slower medium first and lags behind, so the whole wavefront swings round; entering a faster medium swings it the other way.
Marching band view: a row of marchers stepping slantwise from road onto mud slows at one end first and wheels toward the normal; stepping back onto road wheels it away.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: Whenever light goes into something new, it bends toward the normal.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: Most diagrams show air into glass or water, where it really does bend toward the normal.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: The direction matters: going into a rarer medium like air, light speeds up and bends away from the normal.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: Light bends toward the normal entering a denser medium and away from it entering a rarer one.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Refraction visual: drag the ray inside the glass and let it leave into air; it swings away from the normal. Drag it in from air and it swings toward.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: If the angle is big enough, light totally reflects at any surface, from either side.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: Glass and water look shiny from both sides, and 'more than critical' is easy to remember alone.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: From air into glass a refracted ray always exists; only light already in the denser medium can be trapped.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: TIR needs denser-to-rarer travel and an incidence angle above the critical angle.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Refraction visual: inside the glass, drag the ray past the critical angle and watch TIR trap it. Now aim it in from the air side at 80°; it always enters.

contrast_probes.probe: A ray from air hits a pond at 70° to the normal, more than water's critical angle. What happens to it at the surface?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: You expect it to enter and bend toward the normal; good, but would you say the same for a ray leaving water into air?
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You expect it to be totally reflected; check which side of the surface the light starts on, and where it is denser.

contrast_probes.probe: A ray inside glass meets the glass-air surface at 20°. In the air, is its angle from the normal bigger or smaller than 20°?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: You said smaller; ask yourself whether air is denser or rarer than glass, and what that does to the bending.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You said bigger; now, what would happen if that 20° grew past about 42°?

contrast_probes.probe: Can light coming from the air ever be totally internally reflected at a glass surface if you make the angle big enough?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: You said yes; try it in the refraction visual from the air side at 80° and see whether any beam goes into the glass.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: You said no; so what two things must be true for light to get trapped inside the glass?

doubts.q: Does the colour (frequency) of light change when it enters water?
doubts.a: No. Frequency is set by the source and stays the same in every medium. Speed and wavelength both drop by the factor n, which is why a red laser still looks red underwater.

doubts.q: Why doesn't light bend when it hits the surface along the normal?
doubts.a: At 0° incidence, sin i = 0, so Snell's law gives sin r = 0 and the ray goes straight on. It still slows down; only its direction is unchanged.

doubts.q: Can total internal reflection happen when light goes from air into glass?
doubts.a: No. Going from rarer to denser, sin r = sin i / n is always less than 1, so a refracted ray always exists. TIR needs light in the denser medium heading toward a rarer one beyond the critical angle.

doubts.q: Why is it called 'total' if some light reflects at every surface anyway?
doubts.a: Below the critical angle a surface reflects a small part and refracts the rest. Beyond it there is no refracted ray at all, so all the light is reflected, which is why optical fibres lose so little light.
